metadata.title: ericluap/OrderedSemigroups (Lean blueprint)

extraction_notes.note: The proof-sketch rule asks for rigor: semi_formal, but rigor is forbidden on proof nodes (and finalize warns); the chapter-intro sketches were emitted without rigor, with alternative proves edges.
The semigroup chapter says it follows Alimov's paper; only the final theorem TP21 and Alimov's notions are marked external, the blueprint's intermediate lemmas are kept as paper.
Section 1.3 restates both standing assumptions in one sentence; it is recorded as also_stated_at on AssumP1 rather than as a new node.

metadata.extraction_comment: A Lean blueprint: every theorem environment corresponds to a Lean declaration; lemma-like statements are all written as Theorem environments and kept as theorem.

nodes.name: Left ordered group
nodes.statement: A \textbf{left ordered group} $G$ is a group and a partial order such that it is also a left ordered semigroup. In other words, for all $x, y, z \in G$, if $x \le y$, then $z * x \le z * y$.
nodes.genus: a group and a partial order
differentia: if $x \le y$, then $z * x \le z * y$
nodes.label: def:LeftOrderedGroup

nodes.name: Left linear ordered group
nodes.statement: A \textbf{left linear ordered group} $G$ is a left ordered group that is also a linear order.
nodes.label: def:LeftLinearOrderedGroup

nodes.name: Archimedean group
nodes.statement: An \textbf{Archimedean group} is a left ordered group such that for any $g, h \in G$ where $g \ne 1$, there exists an integer $z$ such that $h < g^z$.
differentia: for any $g, h \in G$ where $g \ne 1$, there exists an integer $z$ such that $h < g^z$
nodes.label: def:archimedean_group

nodes.name: Approximation exponent function q
nodes.statement: We define a function $q \colon G \to \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ using \Cref{approximate} such that for any $g\in G$ and $n \in \N$, \[ f^{q_g(n)} \le g^n < f^{q_g(n)+1} \]
nodes.statement_short: $q_g(n)$ is the integer exponent with $f^{q_g(n)} \le g^n < f^{q_g(n)+1}$.
nodes.label: def:q

nodes.name: Map phi to the reals
nodes.statement: We define a map $\phi\colon G \to \R$ by mapping $g$ to the real number that $\frac{q_g(n)}{n}$ converges to as we know from \Cref{q_convergence}.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi(g)$ is the limit of $q_g(n)/n$.
nodes.label: def:phi

nodes.name: Left ordered semigroup
nodes.statement: A \textbf{left ordered semigroup} $S$ is a semigroup and a partial order such that for all $x, y, z\in S$, if $x \le y$, then $z * x \le z * y$.
nodes.genus: a semigroup and a partial order
differentia: if $x \le y$, then $z * x \le z * y$
nodes.label: def:LeftOrderedSemigroup

nodes.name: Right ordered semigroup
nodes.statement: A \textbf{right ordered semigroup} $S$ is a semigroup and a partial order such that for all $x, y, z\in S$, if $x \le y$, then $x * z \le y * z$.
nodes.genus: a semigroup and a partial order
differentia: if $x \le y$, then $x * z \le y * z$
nodes.label: def:RightOrderedSemigroup

nodes.name: Ordered semigroup
nodes.statement: An \textbf{ordered semigroup} $S$ is a left and right ordered semigroup.
nodes.label: def:OrderedSemigroup

nodes.name: Ordered cancel semigroup
nodes.statement: An \textbf{ordered cancel semigroup} $S$ is an ordered semigroup such that for all $a,b,c\in S$, if $a * b \le a * c$ then $b \le c$ and if $b * a \le c * a$ then $b \le c$.
differentia: if $a * b \le a * c$ then $b \le c$
if $b * a \le c * a$ then $b \le c$
nodes.label: def:OrderedCancelSemigroup

nodes.name: Linear ordered semigroup
nodes.statement: A \textbf{linear ordered semigroup} is an ordered semigroup where its partial order is a linear order.
differentia: its partial order is a linear order
nodes.label: def:LinearOrderedSemigroup

nodes.name: Linear ordered cancel semigroup
nodes.statement: A \textbf{linear ordered cancel semigroup} is an ordered cancel semigroup where its partial order is a linear order.
differentia: its partial order is a linear order
nodes.label: def:LinearOrderedCancelSemigroup

nodes.name: Anomalous pair
nodes.statement: An \textbf{anomalous pair} in a left ordered semigroup $S$ is a pair of elements $a,b \in S$ such that for all positive $n \in \mathbb{N}$, either \[ a^n < b^n < a^{n+1} \] or \[ a^n > b^n > a^{n+1} \].
nodes.statement_short: $a,b$ such that $b^n$ lies strictly between $a^n$ and $a^{n+1}$ for every $n$.
nodes.label: def:anomalous_pair

nodes.name: Positive element
nodes.statement: An element $a$ of a left ordered semigroup $S$ is \textbf{positive} if for all $x\in S$, $a*x > x$.
nodes.label: def:positive

nodes.name: Negative element
nodes.statement: An element $a$ of a left ordered semigroup $S$ is \textbf{negative} if for all $x\in S$, $a*x < x$.
nodes.label: def:negative

nodes.name: One element
nodes.statement: An element $a$ of a left ordered semigroup $S$ is \textbf{one} if for all $x\in S$, $a*x = x$.
nodes.label: def:one

nodes.name: Archimedean with respect to
nodes.statement: Let $a$ and $b$ be elements of a left ordered semigroup $S$ that are not one. Then $a$ is said to be \textbf{Archimedean with respect to} $b$ if there exists an $N\in \mathbb{N}^+$ such that for $n > N$, the inequality $b < a^n$ holds if $b$ is positive, and the inequality $b > a^n$ holds if $b$ is negative.
nodes.statement_short: Powers of $a$ eventually exceed $b$ (positive $b$) or go below $b$ (negative $b$).
nodes.label: def:arch_wrt

nodes.name: Archimedean left ordered semigroup
nodes.statement: A left ordered semigroup is \textbf{Archimedean} if any two of its elements of the same sign are mutually Archimedean.
differentia: any two of its elements of the same sign are mutually Archimedean
nodes.label: def:arch

nodes.name: Large differences
nodes.statement: A left ordered semigroup $S$ has \textbf{large differences} if for all $a,b\in S$, the two following implications hold \begin{itemize} \item if $a$ is positive and $a<b$, then there exists $c\in S$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$ such that $c$ is Archimedean with respect to $a$ and $a^n*c \le b^n$ \item if $a$ is negative and $b < a$, then there exists $c\in S$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$ such that $c$ is Archimedean with respect to $a$ and $a^n*c \ge b^n$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: If $a<b$ with $a$ positive (or $b<a$ with $a$ negative), some $c$ Archimedean w.r.t. $a$ fits between $a^n$ and $b^n$.
nodes.label: def:has_large_differences

nodes.name: Approximation of powers by powers of f
nodes.statement: For any $g \in G$ and $p \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists an integer $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that \[ f^q \le g^p < f^{q+1} \]
assumptions: For any $g \in G$ and $p \in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: there exists an integer $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that \[ f^q \le g^p < f^{q+1} \]
nodes.label: approximate

nodes.name: Convergence of almost-additive sequences (Fekete-type lemma)
nodes.statement: For any sequence $a_n$ of real numbers, if there exists $C \in \R$ such that for all $m,n\in \N$ we have that \[ |a_{m+n} - a_m - a_n| \le C \] then sequence $\frac{a_n}{n}$ converges.
assumptions: For any sequence $a_n$ of real numbers
there exists $C \in \R$ such that for all $m,n\in \N$ we have that \[ |a_{m+n} - a_m - a_n| \le C \]
conclusions: sequence $\frac{a_n}{n}$ converges
nodes.statement_short: If $a_n$ is additive up to a bounded error, then $a_n/n$ converges.
nodes.label: sequence_convergence

nodes.name: Exponent additivity bound
nodes.statement: For any $g \in G$ and $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$, we have that \[ f^{q_g(a) + q_g(b)} \le g^{a+b} < f^{q_g(a) + q_g(b) + 2} \]
assumptions: For any $g \in G$ and $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$
nodes.label: q_exp_add

nodes.name: Convergence of q_g(n)/n
nodes.statement: For any $g \in G$, the sequence $\frac{q_g(n)}{n}$ converges.
assumptions: For any $g \in G$
conclusions: the sequence $\frac{q_g(n)}{n}$ converges
nodes.label: q_convergence

nodes.name: Homomorphism case bound for q
nodes.statement: For all $g_1,g_2 \in G$ and $p\in \mathbb{N}$, \[ q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) \le q_{g_1g_2}(p) \le q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) + 1 \]
assumptions: For all $g_1,g_2 \in G$ and $p\in \mathbb{N}$
nodes.statement_short: $q_{g_1g_2}(p)$ equals $q_{g_1}(p)+q_{g_2}(p)$ up to an error of 1.
nodes.label: phi_hom_case

nodes.name: phi is a homomorphism
nodes.statement: The map $\phi$ is a homomorphism.
conclusions: The map $\phi$ is a homomorphism.
nodes.label: phi_hom

nodes.name: phi is order preserving
nodes.statement: For all $g,h \in G$, if $g \le h$ then $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$.
assumptions: For all $g,h \in G$
$g \le h$
conclusions: $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$
nodes.label: order_preserving_phi

nodes.name: phi maps f to one
nodes.statement: We have that $\phi(f) = 1$ where $f$ is our fixed positive element.
assumptions: $f$ is our fixed positive element
nodes.label: f_maps_one

nodes.name: phi is injective
nodes.statement: The map $\phi$ is injective.
conclusions: The map $\phi$ is injective.
nodes.label: injective_phi

nodes.name: phi is strictly order preserving
nodes.statement: For all $g,h \in G$, we have that $g \le h$ if and only if $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$.
assumptions: For all $g,h \in G$
conclusions: $g \le h$ if and only if $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$
nodes.label: strict_order_preserving_phi

nodes.name: Holder's theorem
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a left linear ordered group that is Archimedean, then $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Hölder; proof following Deroin, Navas, Rivas, Groups, Orders, and Dynamics
assumptions: $G$ is a left linear ordered group that is Archimedean
conclusions: $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: holders_theorem

nodes.name: Elements are positive, negative or one
nodes.statement: Each element $a$ of a linear ordered cancel semigroup $S$ is either positive, negative, or one.
assumptions: Each element $a$ of a linear ordered cancel semigroup $S$
conclusions: is either positive, negative, or one
nodes.label: thm:pos_neg_or_one

nodes.name: Non-Archimedean implies anomalous pair
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a non-Archimedean linear ordered cancel semigroup, then there exists an anomalous pair.
assumptions: $S$ is a non-Archimedean linear ordered cancel semigroup
conclusions: there exists an anomalous pair
nodes.label: non_arch_anomalous

nodes.name: No anomalous pairs implies commutative and Archimedean
nodes.statement: A linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs is an Archimedean commutative semigroup.
assumptions: A linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs
conclusions: is an Archimedean commutative semigroup
nodes.label: non_anomalous_comm_and_arch

nodes.name: No anomalous pairs iff large differences
nodes.statement: In a linear ordered cancel semigroup $S$, there are no anomalous pairs if and only if there are large differences.
assumptions: In a linear ordered cancel semigroup $S$
conclusions: there are no anomalous pairs if and only if there are large differences
nodes.label: not_anomalous_iff_large_difference

nodes.name: Embedding into a commutative monoid without anomalous pairs
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs, then there exists a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid $M$ without anomalous pairs such that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $M$.
assumptions: $S$ is a linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs
conclusions: there exists a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid $M$ without anomalous pairs such that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $M$
nodes.label: to_not_anom_monoid

nodes.name: Existence of large positive (negative) elements
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs such that there exists a positive element of $S$. Then for all $x \in S$, there exists a $y \in S$ such that $y$ is positive and $x*y$ is positive. Similarly, if there exists a negative element of $S$ then for all $x \in S$ there exists a $y \in S$ such that $y$ is negative and $x*y$ is negative.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs
there exists a positive element of $S$
if there exists a negative element of $S$
conclusions: for all $x \in S$, there exists a $y \in S$ such that $y$ is positive and $x*y$ is positive
for all $x \in S$ there exists a $y \in S$ such that $y$ is negative and $x*y$ is negative

assumptions: there exists a positive element of $S$
conclusions: for all $x \in S$, there exists a $y \in S$ such that $y$ is positive and $x*y$ is positive

assumptions: if there exists a negative element of $S$
conclusions: for all $x \in S$ there exists a $y \in S$ such that $y$ is negative and $x*y$ is negative

nodes.label: pos_large_elements

nodes.name: Grothendieck group fractions with positive (negative) parts
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid without anomalous pairs and let $G$ be its Grothendieck group. If $M$ has a positive (negative) element, then for any element $\frac{a}{b} \in G$ where $a,b \in M$, there exist $a', b' \in M$ such that $a'$ and $b'$ are positive (negative) and $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{a'}{b'}$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid without anomalous pairs and let $G$ be its Grothendieck group.
$M$ has a positive (negative) element
conclusions: for any element $\frac{a}{b} \in G$ where $a,b \in M$, there exist $a', b' \in M$ such that $a'$ and $b'$ are positive (negative) and $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{a'}{b'}$
nodes.statement_short: Every element of the Grothendieck group is a fraction of two positive (negative) monoid elements.
nodes.label: not_anom_pos_pair

nodes.name: Grothendieck group is Archimedean
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid. If $M$ does not have anomalous pairs, then its Grothendieck group is Archimedean.
assumptions: Let $M$ be a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid.
$M$ does not have anomalous pairs
conclusions: its Grothendieck group is Archimedean
nodes.label: not_anom_to_arch

nodes.name: Embedding into an Archimedean group
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a linear ordered cancel semigroup that does not have anomalous pairs, then there exists a linear ordered commutative group $G$ that is Archimedean such that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $G$.
assumptions: $S$ is a linear ordered cancel semigroup that does not have anomalous pairs
conclusions: there exists a linear ordered commutative group $G$ that is Archimedean such that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $G$
nodes.label: to_arch_group

nodes.name: Holder's theorem for semigroups without anomalous pairs
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs. Then $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of the real numbers.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a linear ordered cancel semigroup without anomalous pairs.
conclusions: $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of the real numbers.
nodes.label: holder_not_anom

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Since $G$ is an Archimedean group, we can construct exponents $l$ and $u$ such that $f^l < g^p < f^u$. Therefore, there must exist some integer $q$ which satisfies what we want.
nodes.statement_short: Archimedean property bounds $g^p$ between powers of $f$; pick the integer $q$ in between.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Not included here as the ideas are separate from this project.
nodes.statement_short: Omitted: not included in the project.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: We know the following two things by the definition of $q$ \begin{align*} f^{q_g(a)}\le &g^a < f^{q_g(a)+1}\\ f^{q_g(b)}\le &g^b < f^{q_g(b)+1}\\ \end{align*} And so it follows that \[ f^{q_g(a)+q_g(b)}\le g^{a+b} < f^{q_g(a)+q_g(b) + 2} \]
nodes.statement_short: Add the two defining inequalities for $q_g(a)$ and $q_g(b)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: From \Cref{q_exp_add}, we have that \[ q_g(a) + q_g(b) \le q_g(a+b) \le q_g(a)+q_g(b) + 1 \] and so \[ |q_g(a+b) - q_g(a) - q_g(b)| \le 1 \] Therefore, by \Cref{sequence_convergence} with $C = 1$, we have that the sequence $\frac{q_g(n)}{n}$ converges.
nodes.statement_short: Almost-additivity of $q_g$ from Theorem 3, then the convergence lemma with $C=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: Let $q_1 = q_{g_1}(p)$ and $q_2 = q_{g_2}(p)$. Then we know that \begin{align*} f^{q_1} \le &g_1^p < f^{q_1+1}\\ f^{q_2} \le &g_2^p < f^{q_2+1}\\ \end{align*} And so we also have the following two facts \begin{align*} f^{q_1+q_2}&\le g_1^p g_2^p\\ g_2^p g_1^p& < f^{q_1 + q_2 + 2} \end{align*} We look at the case where $g_1g_2 \le g_2g_1$. Then $g_1^p g_2^p \le (g_1g_2)^p \le g_2^p g_1^p$. And so combined with the previous facts, we have that \[ f^{q_1+q_2}\le g_1^p g_2^p \le (g_1g_2)^p \le g_2^p g_1^p < f^{q_1+q_2+2} \] Therefore, \[ q_1+q_2 \le q_{g_1g_2}(p) \le q_1+q_2+1 \] And so we are done. The case where $g_2g_1 \le g_1g_2$ follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the defining bounds and split on the order of $g_1g_2$ and $g_2g_1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: Let $g_1, g_2 \in G$. Then from \Cref{phi_hom_case} we have that \[ q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) \le q_{g_1g_2}(p) \le q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) + 1 \] And so since $\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p)}{p} = \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) + 1}{p}$, we have that \[ \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p)}{p} = \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1g_2(p)}}{p} \] Therefore, by the definition of $\phi$, we have shown that $\phi(g_1)+\phi(g_2) = \phi(g_1g_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide the bounds of Theorem 5 by $p$ and take limits.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement: First, notice that since $g\le h$, then for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$, $q_g(p) \le q_h(p)$. Then from the definition of $\phi$, it follows that $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $q_g(p)$ in $g$ passes to the limit.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement: We have that for all $n\in \mathbb{n}$ that $f^n \le f^n < f^{n+1}$ and so $q_f(n) = n$. Therefore, $\phi(f) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $q_f(n) = n$, so the limit is 1.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9
nodes.statement: Since from \Cref{phi_hom} we have that $\phi$ is a homomorphism, it suffices to show that for any $g\in G$, if $\phi(g) = 0$, then $g = 1$. Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists $g \in G$ such that $\phi(g) = 0$ but $g$ is not equal to $1$. Then since $G$ is Archimedean, there exists an integer $z$ such that $g^z > f$. Therefore, since by \Cref{f_maps_one} we have that $\phi(f) = 1$, \begin{align*} 0 &= \phi(g) = \phi(g)^z = \phi(g^z)\\ &> \phi(f) = 1 \end{align*} Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to trivial kernel; by contradiction, an Archimedean power of $g$ exceeds $f$ so $0 > 1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow$) This is \Cref{order_preserving_phi}. ($\Leftarrow$) We have that $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $h < g$. Then by \Cref{order_preserving_phi}, we know that $\phi(h) \le \phi(g)$. Therefore, $\phi(g) = \phi(h)$. And so by \Cref{injective_phi}, we know that $\phi$ is injective and so $g = h$. Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction is order preservation; converse by contradiction using injectivity.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: First, we look at the case where there exists a positive element $f$ in $G$. Given such an element, we have an order preserving, injective homomorphism $\phi$. And so $G$ is isomorphic to the image of $\phi$ which is a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$. If there does not exist a positive element in $G$, then $G$ is trivial and is isomorphic to the trivial subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: If a positive element exists, $\phi$ embeds $G$ into $\mathbb{R}$; otherwise $G$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12
nodes.statement: Let $a\in S$ and $b\in S$. Since the $S$ is a linear order we have one of the following cases. The first case is that $b * a > b$. Then for all $x\in S$ we have that $b * a * x > b * x$ and so $a * x > x$. Therefore, $a$ is positive. The second case is that $b * a < b$. Then for all $x\in S$ we have that $b * a * x < b * x$ and so $a * x < x$. Therefore, $a$ is negative. The last case is that $b * a = b$. Then for all $x\in S$ we have that $b * a * x = b * x$ and so $a * x = x$. Therefore, $a$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $b*a$ with $b$ and cancel $b$ in each of the three cases.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 13
nodes.statement: Since $S$ is non-Archimedean, there exists $a,b\in S$ such that $a$ and $b$ have the sign and are not mutually Archimedean. First, we look at the case where $a$ and $b$ are positive. Then since they are not mutually Archimedean, without loss of generality, for all $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$, $a^n < b$. Then we either have that $a * b \le b * a$ or that $b*a\le a * b$. In the first case, we have that \[ a^n + b^n \le (a*b)^n \le b^n + a^n \] which means that, since $a^n < b$, \[ b^n < (a*b)^n < b^{n+1} \] And so $b$ and $a*b$ form an anomalous pair. The other cases follow similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Take two non-mutually-Archimedean elements and show $b$ and $a*b$ form an anomalous pair.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 14
nodes.statement: Let $a$ and $b$ be elements of an ordered semigroup $S$. If either $a$ or $b$ is one, then they commute. We begin with the case that $a$ and $b$ are positive. If $a * b < b * a$, then for all $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$, we have that \begin{align*} (a*b)^{n+1} &= a * (b*a)^n * b \\ &> (b*a)^n * b \\ &> (b*a)^n \\ &> (a*b)^n \end{align*} And so $a*b$ and $b*a$ form an anomalous pair. The same for the case that $b * a < a * b$. Therefore, we must have that $a*b = b*a$. The case where $a$ and $b$ are negative follows similarly. We now look at the case where $a$ is negative and $b$ is positive. If the element $1$ exists and $a*b = 1$, then $a * b * a = a$ and so $b*a = 1$. Therefore, $a$ and $b$ commute. If $a * b$ is positive, then \begin{align*} (a*b) * (a*b) &> a * b \\ (b * a) * b &> b \\ b * a &> 0 \end{align*} We already showed that positive elements commute and so \[ (b*a) * b = b * (b * a)\] Now we look at the case where $a*b < b*a$. Then we have that \begin{align*} (a * b)^2 &= a * ((b*a) * b) \\ &= a * (b * (b * a)) \\ &= (a * b) * (b * a) \\ &> (a * b) * (a * b) \\ &= (a * b)^2 \end{align*} Which is a contradiction. We get a similar contradiction in the case that $b*a < a*b$. Therefore, $a*b = b*a$. The case where $a*b$ is negative follows similarly. The case where $b$ is negative and $a$ is positive is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on signs; non-commuting pairs yield anomalous pairs or contradictions. The mixed-sign case reuses commutativity of positive elements.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 15
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow$) If $a$ and $b$ are positive and $a < b$, then we have that $a^n < b^n$ for all $n$. Therefore, there must exist an $n$ such that $a^{n+1} \le b^n$ as otherwise $a$ and $b$ would form an anomalous pair. Thus, the theorem is satisfied with $c = a$. Similarly if $a$ and $b$ are negatiave. ($\Leftarrow$) We look first at the case where $a$ and $b$ are positive and $a < b$. Then we have $c\in S$ Archimedean with respect to $a$ and $m\in \mathbb{N}^+$ such that $a^m * c \le b^m$. Therefore, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}^+$, either \[(a^m)^n * c^n \le (a^m*c)^n \le (b^m)^n\] or \[c^n * (a^m)^n \le (a^m*c)^n \le (b^m)^n\] holds. Since $c$ is Archimedean with respect to $a$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $a < c^n$. Thus, for any $n \ge N$, we get from the previous relations that \[a^{mn + 1} \le b^{mn}\] and so $a$ and $b$ do not form an anomalous pair. Similalry if $a$ and $b$ are negative.
nodes.statement_short: Forward: absence of anomalous pair gives $a^{n+1} \le b^n$, take $c=a$. Converse: powers of $c$ separate $a^{mn}$ from $b^{mn}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 16
nodes.statement: We do casework on whether or not $S$ has an element that is one. If $S$ has an element that is one then it is already a monoid. Furthermore, since it has no anomalous pairs, by \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch}, it is commutative. And so we are done. If $S$ does not have an element that is one, then we let $M$ be $S$ with one added. We define one to be less than every positive element and greater than every negative element. By \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch}, we know that $S$ is commutative and so $M$ is too. Furthermore, it is clear that $M$ has no anomalous pairs still. Then $S$ is isomorphic to the subsemigroup of $M$ that is all its elements except for the added one.
nodes.statement_short: Casework on whether $S$ has a one; if not, adjoin one ordered between positives and negatives.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 17
nodes.statement: We look at the positive case. If $x$ is positive then we are done as $x*x$ is positive. Next we look at the case where $x$ is negative. Assume for the sake of contradiction that for all $y \in S$, if $y$ is positive then $x*y$ is negative. Let $z$ be a positive element we assumed existed in $S$. Then for all positive $n \in \N$, we have that $x * z^{n+2}$ is negative. Recall that from \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch} we have commutativity. From there we have an anomalous pair: \begin{align*} (x * z)^n &= x^n * z^n \ge x^n\\ &\ge x^n * (x * z^{n+2})\\ &= (x * z)^{n+1} * z > (x*z)^{n+1} \end{align*} Contradiction. And similarly for the negative case.
nodes.statement_short: Positive $x$ is trivial; for negative $x$, by contradiction build an anomalous pair from $x*z$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 18
nodes.statement: Let $\frac{a}{b}\in G$ where $a,b\in M$. Since $M$ has a positive element, by \Cref{pos_large_elements}, we have $a_2, b_2\in M$ such that $a*a_2$ and $b*b_2$ are positive. Let $a' = a*a_2$ and $b' = b*b_2$. Then $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{a'}{b'}$ and $a'$ and $b'$ are positive. And similarly for the negative case.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply numerator and denominator by elements from Theorem 17 making them positive.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 19
nodes.statement: If $M$ is trivial then we are done. Otherwise, it has a positive element of a negative element. We look at the case where $M$ has a positive element $t$. We now want to show that the Grothendieck group $G$ of $M$ is Archimedean. It suffices to show that for any positive $g, h \in G$, there exists an integer $n$ such that $g^n > h$. Since $g, h \in G$, there exist $g_1,g_2,h_1,h_2 \in M$ such that $g = \frac{g_1}{g_2}$ and $h = \frac{h_1}{h_2}$, and by \Cref{not_anom_pos_pair}, we can assume that $g_1$, $g_2$, $h_1$, and $h_2$ are positive. Then since $M$ does not have anomalous pairs, we have by \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch} that $M$ is Archimedean. Since $g_1$ and $h_1$ are positive and $M$ is Archimedean, there exists a positive $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $g_2^n > h_1$. So in particular, we have that $g_2^N > h_1$. Notice that since $\frac{g_1}{g_2}$ positive, we have that $g_2 < g_1$. And therefore, since $M$ does not have anomalous pairs, there exists a positive natural number $N_1$ such that $g_2^{N_1+N} < g_1^{N_1}$. We now claim that $g^{N_1} > h$. This is equivalent to showing that $g_2^{N_1}*h_1 < h_2*g_1^{N_1}$. And we have that \begin{align*} g_2^{N_1} * h_1 &= h_1 * g_2^{N_1}\\ &< g_2^N * g_2^{N_1} = g_2^{N_1 + N}\\ &< g_1^{N_1} \\ &< h_1 * g_1^{N_1} \end{align*} And so we are done. The final case where $M$ has a negative element follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Write $g,h$ as fractions of positive elements and use Archimedeanity and large differences in $M$ to get $g^{N_1} > h$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 20
nodes.statement: By \Cref{to_not_anom_monoid}, we have that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid $M$ that does not have anomalous pairs. We let $G$ be the Grothendieck group of $M$. Then by \Cref{not_anom_to_arch} we know that $G$ is Archimedean. Since $G$ is the Grothendieck group of $M$, $M$ is isomorphic to a submonoid of $G$. Thus, we have that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $S$ into the monoid $M$, then into its Archimedean Grothendieck group.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 21
nodes.statement: By \Cref{to_arch_group}, there exists a linear ordered commutative Archimedean group $G$ such that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $G$. By \Cref{holders_theorem}, $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\R$. Therefore, $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $\R$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $S$ in an Archimedean group, then apply Holder's theorem for groups.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Holder's theorem
nodes.statement: We choose an element of the ordered group $f$ and map it to $1$ in the real numbers. Then for any other element $g$ of the ordered group, we use $f$ to construct a sequence of rational approximations of $g$. We map $g$ to the real number that is the limit of this sequence of approximations. We then prove that this map is injective and order preserving.
nodes.statement_short: Send a fixed positive $f$ to 1 and $g$ to the limit of rational approximations; show the map is injective and order preserving.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Holder's theorem for semigroups
nodes.statement: We show that if a a linear ordered cancel semigroup does not have anomalous pairs, then there exists a larger Archimedean group containing it. Then from Holder's theorem for groups, that larger group is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ and so the smaller semigroup is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed the semigroup in an Archimedean group, then apply Holder's theorem for groups.

nodes.name: Standing assumption: G left linear ordered Archimedean
nodes.statement: In this section we assume that $G$ is a left linear ordered group that is Archimedean.
also_stated_at: So we assume that $G$ is a left linear ordered group that is Archimedean, $f\in G$, and $1 < f$.

nodes.name: Standing assumption: fixed element f > 1
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we assume we have an element $f\in G$ such that $1 < f$.

nodes.name: Intuition for anomalous pairs
nodes.statement: Intuitively, an anomalous pair represents a pair of elements that are infinitely close. If you have two real numbers $s$ and $r$ such that $s < r$, then as $n \in \N$ gets larger, $n\cdot s$ and $n\cdot r$ get farther apart. However, for an anomalous pair, the elements always remain close to each other.
nodes.statement_short: Anomalous pairs are infinitely close elements, unlike distinct reals whose multiples drift apart.

nodes.name: Intuition for large differences
nodes.statement: Intuitively, this is saying if $a < b$ then eventually $a^n$ is significantly smaller than $b^n$. Here ``significantly smaller'' means that there is an element that is not infinitely small with respect to $a$ that separates $a^n$ and $b$.
nodes.statement_short: Large differences means $a^n$ eventually falls well below $b^n$, separated by a non-infinitesimal element.

nodes.name: Name the exponents and multiply their defining bounds
nodes.statement: Let $q_1 = q_{g_1}(p)$ and $q_2 = q_{g_2}(p)$. Then we know that \begin{align*} f^{q_1} \le &g_1^p < f^{q_1+1}\\ f^{q_2} \le &g_2^p < f^{q_2+1}\\ \end{align*} And so we also have the following two facts \begin{align*} f^{q_1+q_2}&\le g_1^p g_2^p\\ g_2^p g_1^p& < f^{q_1 + q_2 + 2} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Name the exponents and multiply their defining bounds.

nodes.name: Case $g_1g_2 \le g_2g_1$: sandwich $(g_1g_2)^p$
nodes.statement: We look at the case where $g_1g_2 \le g_2g_1$. Then $g_1^p g_2^p \le (g_1g_2)^p \le g_2^p g_1^p$. And so combined with the previous facts, we have that \[ f^{q_1+q_2}\le g_1^p g_2^p \le (g_1g_2)^p \le g_2^p g_1^p < f^{q_1+q_2+2} \]
nodes.statement_short: Case $g_1g_2 \le g_2g_1$: sandwich $(g_1g_2)^p$.

nodes.name: Read off the exponent bounds; other case symmetric
nodes.statement: Therefore, \[ q_1+q_2 \le q_{g_1g_2}(p) \le q_1+q_2+1 \] And so we are done. The case where $g_2g_1 \le g_1g_2$ follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Read off the exponent bounds; other case symmetric.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 5 to $g_1,g_2$
nodes.statement: Let $g_1, g_2 \in G$. Then from \Cref{phi_hom_case} we have that \[ q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) \le q_{g_1g_2}(p) \le q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) + 1 \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 5 to $g_1,g_2$.

nodes.name: Squeeze: both bounds have the same limit after dividing by $p$
nodes.statement: And so since $\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p)}{p} = \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p) + 1}{p}$, we have that \[ \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1}(p) + q_{g_2}(p)}{p} = \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{q_{g_1g_2(p)}}{p} \]
nodes.statement_short: Squeeze: both bounds have the same limit after dividing by $p$.

nodes.name: Conclude additivity of $\phi$
nodes.statement: Therefore, by the definition of $\phi$, we have shown that $\phi(g_1)+\phi(g_2) = \phi(g_1g_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude additivity of $\phi$.

nodes.name: Reduce injectivity to trivial kernel
nodes.statement: Since from \Cref{phi_hom} we have that $\phi$ is a homomorphism, it suffices to show that for any $g\in G$, if $\phi(g) = 0$, then $g = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce injectivity to trivial kernel.

nodes.name: Suppose $\phi(g)=0$ with $g \ne 1$
nodes.statement: Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists $g \in G$ such that $\phi(g) = 0$ but $g$ is not equal to $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose $\phi(g)=0$ with $g \ne 1$.

nodes.name: Archimedean property gives $g^z > f$
nodes.statement: Then since $G$ is Archimedean, there exists an integer $z$ such that $g^z > f$.
nodes.statement_short: Archimedean property gives $g^z > f$.

nodes.name: Apply $\phi$ to get $0 > 1$
nodes.statement: Therefore, since by \Cref{f_maps_one} we have that $\phi(f) = 1$, \begin{align*} 0 &= \phi(g) = \phi(g)^z = \phi(g^z)\\ &> \phi(f) = 1 \end{align*} Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\phi$ to get $0 > 1$.

nodes.name: Forward direction is Theorem 7
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow$) This is \Cref{order_preserving_phi}.
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction is Theorem 7.

nodes.name: Converse by contradiction
nodes.statement: ($\Leftarrow$) We have that $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $h < g$. Then by \Cref{order_preserving_phi}, we know that $\phi(h) \le \phi(g)$. Therefore, $\phi(g) = \phi(h)$. And so by \Cref{injective_phi}, we know that $\phi$ is injective and so $g = h$. Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Converse by contradiction.

nodes.name: Assume $h < g$
nodes.statement: ($\Leftarrow$) We have that $\phi(g) \le \phi(h)$. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $h < g$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $h < g$.

nodes.name: Order preservation forces $\phi(g)=\phi(h)$
nodes.statement: Then by \Cref{order_preserving_phi}, we know that $\phi(h) \le \phi(g)$. Therefore, $\phi(g) = \phi(h)$.
nodes.statement_short: Order preservation forces $\phi(g)=\phi(h)$.

nodes.name: Injectivity gives $g=h$, contradiction
nodes.statement: And so by \Cref{injective_phi}, we know that $\phi$ is injective and so $g = h$. Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity gives $g=h$, contradiction.

nodes.name: Positive element exists: $\phi$ is an order-preserving embedding
nodes.statement: First, we look at the case where there exists a positive element $f$ in $G$. Given such an element, we have an order preserving, injective homomorphism $\phi$. And so $G$ is isomorphic to the image of $\phi$ which is a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Positive element exists: $\phi$ is an order-preserving embedding.

nodes.name: No positive element: $G$ is trivial
nodes.statement: If there does not exist a positive element in $G$, then $G$ is trivial and is isomorphic to the trivial subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: No positive element: $G$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Fix $a,b$ and split by linearity on $b*a$ versus $b$
nodes.statement: Let $a\in S$ and $b\in S$. Since the $S$ is a linear order we have one of the following cases.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $a,b$ and split by linearity on $b*a$ versus $b$.

nodes.name: Case $b*a > b$: cancel to get $a$ positive
nodes.statement: The first case is that $b * a > b$. Then for all $x\in S$ we have that $b * a * x > b * x$ and so $a * x > x$. Therefore, $a$ is positive.
nodes.statement_short: Case $b*a > b$: cancel to get $a$ positive.

nodes.name: Case $b*a < b$: $a$ negative
nodes.statement: The second case is that $b * a < b$. Then for all $x\in S$ we have that $b * a * x < b * x$ and so $a * x < x$. Therefore, $a$ is negative.
nodes.statement_short: Case $b*a < b$: $a$ negative.

nodes.name: Case $b*a = b$: $a$ is one
nodes.statement: The last case is that $b * a = b$. Then for all $x\in S$ we have that $b * a * x = b * x$ and so $a * x = x$. Therefore, $a$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Case $b*a = b$: $a$ is one.

nodes.name: Pick $a,b$ of the same sign, not mutually Archimedean
nodes.statement: Since $S$ is non-Archimedean, there exists $a,b\in S$ such that $a$ and $b$ have the sign and are not mutually Archimedean.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $a,b$ of the same sign, not mutually Archimedean.

nodes.name: Positive case: WLOG $a^n < b$ for all $n$
nodes.statement: First, we look at the case where $a$ and $b$ are positive. Then since they are not mutually Archimedean, without loss of generality, for all $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$, $a^n < b$.
nodes.statement_short: Positive case: WLOG $a^n < b$ for all $n$.

nodes.name: Sandwich $(a*b)^n$ between $b^n$ and $b^{n+1}$: anomalous pair
nodes.statement: Then we either have that $a * b \le b * a$ or that $b*a\le a * b$. In the first case, we have that \[ a^n + b^n \le (a*b)^n \le b^n + a^n \] which means that, since $a^n < b$, \[ b^n < (a*b)^n < b^{n+1} \] And so $b$ and $a*b$ form an anomalous pair. The other cases follow similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $(a*b)^n$ between $b^n$ and $b^{n+1}$: anomalous pair.

nodes.name: If either element is one, they commute
nodes.statement: Let $a$ and $b$ be elements of an ordered semigroup $S$. If either $a$ or $b$ is one, then they commute.
nodes.statement_short: If either element is one, they commute.

nodes.name: Same-sign case: positive elements commute
nodes.statement: We begin with the case that $a$ and $b$ are positive. If $a * b < b * a$, then for all $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$, we have that \begin{align*} (a*b)^{n+1} &= a * (b*a)^n * b \\ &> (b*a)^n * b \\ &> (b*a)^n \\ &> (a*b)^n \end{align*} And so $a*b$ and $b*a$ form an anomalous pair. The same for the case that $b * a < a * b$. Therefore, we must have that $a*b = b*a$. The case where $a$ and $b$ are negative follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Same-sign case: positive elements commute.

nodes.name: If $a*b<b*a$, $a*b$ and $b*a$ form an anomalous pair
nodes.statement: We begin with the case that $a$ and $b$ are positive. If $a * b < b * a$, then for all $n\in \mathbb{N}^+$, we have that \begin{align*} (a*b)^{n+1} &= a * (b*a)^n * b \\ &> (b*a)^n * b \\ &> (b*a)^n \\ &> (a*b)^n \end{align*} And so $a*b$ and $b*a$ form an anomalous pair.
nodes.statement_short: If $a*b<b*a$, $a*b$ and $b*a$ form an anomalous pair.

nodes.name: Hence $a*b=b*a$; negative case similar
nodes.statement: The same for the case that $b * a < a * b$. Therefore, we must have that $a*b = b*a$. The case where $a$ and $b$ are negative follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $a*b=b*a$; negative case similar.

nodes.name: Mixed-sign case
nodes.statement: We now look at the case where $a$ is negative and $b$ is positive. If the element $1$ exists and $a*b = 1$, then $a * b * a = a$ and so $b*a = 1$. Therefore, $a$ and $b$ commute. If $a * b$ is positive, then \begin{align*} (a*b) * (a*b) &> a * b \\ (b * a) * b &> b \\ b * a &> 0 \end{align*} We already showed that positive elements commute and so \[ (b*a) * b = b * (b * a)\] Now we look at the case where $a*b < b*a$. Then we have that \begin{align*} (a * b)^2 &= a * ((b*a) * b) \\ &= a * (b * (b * a)) \\ &= (a * b) * (b * a) \\ &> (a * b) * (a * b) \\ &= (a * b)^2 \end{align*} Which is a contradiction. We get a similar contradiction in the case that $b*a < a*b$. Therefore, $a*b = b*a$. The case where $a*b$ is negative follows similarly. The case where $b$ is negative and $a$ is positive is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Mixed-sign case.

nodes.name: Subcase $a*b=1$: they commute
nodes.statement: We now look at the case where $a$ is negative and $b$ is positive. If the element $1$ exists and $a*b = 1$, then $a * b * a = a$ and so $b*a = 1$. Therefore, $a$ and $b$ commute.
nodes.statement_short: Subcase $a*b=1$: they commute.

nodes.name: Subcase $a*b$ positive: $b*a$ is positive
nodes.statement: If $a * b$ is positive, then \begin{align*} (a*b) * (a*b) &> a * b \\ (b * a) * b &> b \\ b * a &> 0 \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Subcase $a*b$ positive: $b*a$ is positive.

nodes.name: Use commutativity of positive elements
nodes.statement: We already showed that positive elements commute and so \[ (b*a) * b = b * (b * a)\]
nodes.statement_short: Use commutativity of positive elements.

nodes.name: Non-commuting yields $(a*b)^2 > (a*b)^2$; remaining cases similar
nodes.statement: Now we look at the case where $a*b < b*a$. Then we have that \begin{align*} (a * b)^2 &= a * ((b*a) * b) \\ &= a * (b * (b * a)) \\ &= (a * b) * (b * a) \\ &> (a * b) * (a * b) \\ &= (a * b)^2 \end{align*} Which is a contradiction. We get a similar contradiction in the case that $b*a < a*b$. Therefore, $a*b = b*a$. The case where $a*b$ is negative follows similarly. The case where $b$ is negative and $a$ is positive is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Non-commuting yields $(a*b)^2 > (a*b)^2$; remaining cases similar.

nodes.name: No anomalous pairs gives $a^{n+1} \le b^n$; take $c=a$
nodes.statement: ($\Rightarrow$) If $a$ and $b$ are positive and $a < b$, then we have that $a^n < b^n$ for all $n$. Therefore, there must exist an $n$ such that $a^{n+1} \le b^n$ as otherwise $a$ and $b$ would form an anomalous pair. Thus, the theorem is satisfied with $c = a$. Similarly if $a$ and $b$ are negatiave.
nodes.statement_short: No anomalous pairs gives $a^{n+1} \le b^n$; take $c=a$.

nodes.name: Large differences rule out anomalous pairs
nodes.statement: ($\Leftarrow$) We look first at the case where $a$ and $b$ are positive and $a < b$. Then we have $c\in S$ Archimedean with respect to $a$ and $m\in \mathbb{N}^+$ such that $a^m * c \le b^m$. Therefore, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}^+$, either \[(a^m)^n * c^n \le (a^m*c)^n \le (b^m)^n\] or \[c^n * (a^m)^n \le (a^m*c)^n \le (b^m)^n\] holds. Since $c$ is Archimedean with respect to $a$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $a < c^n$. Thus, for any $n \ge N$, we get from the previous relations that \[a^{mn + 1} \le b^{mn}\] and so $a$ and $b$ do not form an anomalous pair. Similalry if $a$ and $b$ are negative.
nodes.statement_short: Large differences rule out anomalous pairs.

nodes.name: Large differences give $c$ and $m$ with $a^m*c \le b^m$
nodes.statement: ($\Leftarrow$) We look first at the case where $a$ and $b$ are positive and $a < b$. Then we have $c\in S$ Archimedean with respect to $a$ and $m\in \mathbb{N}^+$ such that $a^m * c \le b^m$.
nodes.statement_short: Large differences give $c$ and $m$ with $a^m*c \le b^m$.

nodes.name: Raise to the $n$-th power
nodes.statement: Therefore, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}^+$, either \[(a^m)^n * c^n \le (a^m*c)^n \le (b^m)^n\] or \[c^n * (a^m)^n \le (a^m*c)^n \le (b^m)^n\] holds.
nodes.statement_short: Raise to the $n$-th power.

nodes.name: Archimedean $c$ gives $a^{mn+1} \le b^{mn}$, so no anomalous pair
nodes.statement: Since $c$ is Archimedean with respect to $a$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $a < c^n$. Thus, for any $n \ge N$, we get from the previous relations that \[a^{mn + 1} \le b^{mn}\] and so $a$ and $b$ do not form an anomalous pair. Similalry if $a$ and $b$ are negative.
nodes.statement_short: Archimedean $c$ gives $a^{mn+1} \le b^{mn}$, so no anomalous pair.

nodes.name: Split on whether $S$ has a one
nodes.statement: We do casework on whether or not $S$ has an element that is one.
nodes.statement_short: Split on whether $S$ has a one.

nodes.name: With a one, $S$ is already a commutative monoid
nodes.statement: If $S$ has an element that is one then it is already a monoid. Furthermore, since it has no anomalous pairs, by \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch}, it is commutative. And so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: With a one, $S$ is already a commutative monoid.

nodes.name: Otherwise adjoin a one between negatives and positives
nodes.statement: If $S$ does not have an element that is one, then we let $M$ be $S$ with one added. We define one to be less than every positive element and greater than every negative element. By \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch}, we know that $S$ is commutative and so $M$ is too. Furthermore, it is clear that $M$ has no anomalous pairs still. Then $S$ is isomorphic to the subsemigroup of $M$ that is all its elements except for the added one.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise adjoin a one between negatives and positives.

nodes.name: Positive $x$: take $y=x$
nodes.statement: We look at the positive case. If $x$ is positive then we are done as $x*x$ is positive.
nodes.statement_short: Positive $x$: take $y=x$.

nodes.name: Negative $x$: contradiction via anomalous pair
nodes.statement: Next we look at the case where $x$ is negative. Assume for the sake of contradiction that for all $y \in S$, if $y$ is positive then $x*y$ is negative. Let $z$ be a positive element we assumed existed in $S$. Then for all positive $n \in \N$, we have that $x * z^{n+2}$ is negative. Recall that from \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch} we have commutativity. From there we have an anomalous pair: \begin{align*} (x * z)^n &= x^n * z^n \ge x^n\\ &\ge x^n * (x * z^{n+2})\\ &= (x * z)^{n+1} * z > (x*z)^{n+1} \end{align*} Contradiction. And similarly for the negative case.
nodes.statement_short: Negative $x$: contradiction via anomalous pair.

nodes.name: Assume $x*y$ negative for every positive $y$
nodes.statement: Next we look at the case where $x$ is negative. Assume for the sake of contradiction that for all $y \in S$, if $y$ is positive then $x*y$ is negative.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $x*y$ negative for every positive $y$.

nodes.name: Fix positive $z$; $x*z^{n+2}$ is negative
nodes.statement: Let $z$ be a positive element we assumed existed in $S$. Then for all positive $n \in \N$, we have that $x * z^{n+2}$ is negative.
nodes.statement_short: Fix positive $z$; $x*z^{n+2}$ is negative.

nodes.name: Recall commutativity
nodes.statement: Recall that from \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch} we have commutativity.
nodes.statement_short: Recall commutativity.

nodes.name: Commutativity gives an anomalous pair, contradiction
nodes.statement: From there we have an anomalous pair: \begin{align*} (x * z)^n &= x^n * z^n \ge x^n\\ &\ge x^n * (x * z^{n+2})\\ &= (x * z)^{n+1} * z > (x*z)^{n+1} \end{align*} Contradiction. And similarly for the negative case.
nodes.statement_short: Commutativity gives an anomalous pair, contradiction.

nodes.name: Theorem 17 gives $a_2,b_2$ making $a*a_2$, $b*b_2$ positive
nodes.statement: Let $\frac{a}{b}\in G$ where $a,b\in M$. Since $M$ has a positive element, by \Cref{pos_large_elements}, we have $a_2, b_2\in M$ such that $a*a_2$ and $b*b_2$ are positive.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 17 gives $a_2,b_2$ making $a*a_2$, $b*b_2$ positive.

nodes.name: Rewrite the fraction with the positive elements
nodes.statement: Let $a' = a*a_2$ and $b' = b*b_2$. Then $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{a'}{b'}$ and $a'$ and $b'$ are positive. And similarly for the negative case.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the fraction with the positive elements.

nodes.name: Trivial $M$ is immediate; otherwise a sign exists
nodes.statement: If $M$ is trivial then we are done. Otherwise, it has a positive element of a negative element.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial $M$ is immediate; otherwise a sign exists.

nodes.name: Reduce to $g^n > h$ for positive fractions of positive elements
nodes.statement: We look at the case where $M$ has a positive element $t$. We now want to show that the Grothendieck group $G$ of $M$ is Archimedean. It suffices to show that for any positive $g, h \in G$, there exists an integer $n$ such that $g^n > h$. Since $g, h \in G$, there exist $g_1,g_2,h_1,h_2 \in M$ such that $g = \frac{g_1}{g_2}$ and $h = \frac{h_1}{h_2}$, and by \Cref{not_anom_pos_pair}, we can assume that $g_1$, $g_2$, $h_1$, and $h_2$ are positive.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $g^n > h$ for positive fractions of positive elements.

nodes.name: Archimedeanity of $M$ gives $g_2^N > h_1$
nodes.statement: Then since $M$ does not have anomalous pairs, we have by \Cref{non_anomalous_comm_and_arch} that $M$ is Archimedean. Since $g_1$ and $h_1$ are positive and $M$ is Archimedean, there exists a positive $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $g_2^n > h_1$. So in particular, we have that $g_2^N > h_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Archimedeanity of $M$ gives $g_2^N > h_1$.

nodes.name: No anomalous pairs gives $N_1$ with $g_2^{N_1+N} < g_1^{N_1}$
nodes.statement: Notice that since $\frac{g_1}{g_2}$ positive, we have that $g_2 < g_1$. And therefore, since $M$ does not have anomalous pairs, there exists a positive natural number $N_1$ such that $g_2^{N_1+N} < g_1^{N_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: No anomalous pairs gives $N_1$ with $g_2^{N_1+N} < g_1^{N_1}$.

nodes.name: Claim $g^{N_1} > h$ and verify it
nodes.statement: We now claim that $g^{N_1} > h$. This is equivalent to showing that $g_2^{N_1}*h_1 < h_2*g_1^{N_1}$. And we have that \begin{align*} g_2^{N_1} * h_1 &= h_1 * g_2^{N_1}\\ &< g_2^N * g_2^{N_1} = g_2^{N_1 + N}\\ &< g_1^{N_1} \\ &< h_1 * g_1^{N_1} \end{align*} And so we are done. The final case where $M$ has a negative element follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Claim $g^{N_1} > h$ and verify it.

nodes.name: Clear denominators
nodes.statement: This is equivalent to showing that $g_2^{N_1}*h_1 < h_2*g_1^{N_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Clear denominators.

nodes.name: Chain of inequalities; negative case similar
nodes.statement: And we have that \begin{align*} g_2^{N_1} * h_1 &= h_1 * g_2^{N_1}\\ &< g_2^N * g_2^{N_1} = g_2^{N_1 + N}\\ &< g_1^{N_1} \\ &< h_1 * g_1^{N_1} \end{align*} And so we are done. The final case where $M$ has a negative element follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of inequalities; negative case similar.

nodes.name: Embed $S$ into a monoid $M$ without anomalous pairs
nodes.statement: By \Cref{to_not_anom_monoid}, we have that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of a linear ordered cancel commutative monoid $M$ that does not have anomalous pairs.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $S$ into a monoid $M$ without anomalous pairs.

nodes.name: Its Grothendieck group $G$ is Archimedean
nodes.statement: We let $G$ be the Grothendieck group of $M$. Then by \Cref{not_anom_to_arch} we know that $G$ is Archimedean.
nodes.statement_short: Its Grothendieck group $G$ is Archimedean.

nodes.name: Compose the embeddings
nodes.statement: Since $G$ is the Grothendieck group of $M$, $M$ is isomorphic to a submonoid of $G$. Thus, we have that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the embeddings.

nodes.name: Embed in an Archimedean group
nodes.statement: By \Cref{to_arch_group}, there exists a linear ordered commutative Archimedean group $G$ such that $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed in an Archimedean group.

nodes.name: Apply Holder's theorem
nodes.statement: By \Cref{holders_theorem}, $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\R$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Holder's theorem.

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: Therefore, $S$ is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of $\R$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose.
